utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, here we go again. Joanna Korner, together with Anna Richterova, assisted by case manager who is standing in for Ms. Gustin, Mr. Hasan Younis. And good afternoon to you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Trbojevic, my co-counsel, and Marela Jevtovic. Nice to be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Ms. Natasha Fauveau assisted by our case manager, Ms. Tatjana Cmeric for General Talic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you too. Welcome back. I hope you have had a good and relaxing break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from the weather, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can't complain on my part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We do all think we should have gone to Malta for the holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was splendid this time. And not too hot. But anyway after a month you get a little bit sick and tired of it because it tends to be too hot. But coming back, I came for lightning and thunder and lightning on Tuesday morning. It was -- anyway, welcome back. And before I ask you whether you have any preliminaries, I just have some very brief information to give you, and that is more or less I wanted to inform you that all the motions -- all the pending motions - and there aren't many but there are a few - are being dealt with. There is in particular the one relating to 92 bis protective measures, the ones relating to these two respectively are already drafted, in drafted form. We will be meeting throughout this week to discuss them. And then we should be in a position to hand down the decisions in the course of this week, not necessarily at the end of the week, perhaps even -- even before, so that -- I wanted you to know there are some other matters that will be dealt with but not necessarily this week, one of which is the contempt of court issue. And in that respect, I would like to have an indication from all interested parties as to whether we can consider the written phase now closed and proceed with our decision. I would like to have a feedback on this matter. Perhaps I can ask Mr. Ackerman to refer this to his colleague. I would imagine that the written phase, written pleadings phase is concluded as well. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have to say I haven't yet -- I only -- like Your Honour, I came back in the midst of this downpour on Saturday and I haven't had an opportunity to go through all the various documents. But I noticed that Mr. Shellow had sent in what purported to be a response to our simple indication of what the legal researchers had shown, which in fact is a legal -- it's an argument, and it's an argument, as I say, when Mr. Shellow appeared that really should only have been raised in the event that there was a full hearing of contempt. I mean, this is one of the problems. So I'm not sure how Your Honour is going to treat that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't gone through that document at yet --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to be sincere with you. The reason is that what had already come in before or until the time of my departure, end of July, I took with me to Malta to read. What was introduced after that, after then, I gave instructions to keep here, also because I don't -- in summer I don't reside in my usual residence, and I didn't want to have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm having difficulty to hear what Your Honour said, because I can hear some sort of commentary going on. Oh, of course it's for the Milosevic trial. That's what's happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, that part of the documents I haven't gone through as yet. There are two sets, I think, of documents that I've still got to read. I had them filed this morning, but I will be going through them in the course of this week. I don't -- I haven't had time to consult my two colleagues as to whether they have read these documents. I don't know what the position is, but we will -- I think from what I could see, I think I should consider -- we should consider the written pleadings phase to have come to an end, to have been concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's -- Your Honour, that's the only reason I'm raising it, because what Mr. Shellow has done in my opinion is advance an argument on the facts and on various aspects which if, as I said to Your Honour at the time, this is to -- there is a sort of referral for some sort of a hearing, that I would have answered, because there are merits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I think, Ms. Korner, we had made ourselves clear as to where the line of demarcation pertinent to this preliminary hearing, sort of, where the boundaries were. And we do not intend to go beyond those boundaries in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then I think the best thing would be if Your Honour were to be -- Your Honours, I'm sorry, were to be given an opportunity to look at what Mr. Shellow has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if you would be kind enough to let us know how you would treat that particular submission, which does not deal with what were purely submissions of the law that we put before Your Honour without, as we said in our motion, going into anything to do with the merits or the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. More or less, that's it. If -- I'm just asking. Initially way back in January of this year, you will recall that there was an issue related to what would happen to a statement made to the Prosecution by a witness who is now deceased. And we had agreed to have that matter postponed -- the discussion on that matter postponed. What -- what is the position now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that, I think, both ourselves and Madam Fauveau, whom it affects, thought it would be appropriate to deal with it after Colonel Selak has testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still the same --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's still the say. Which would be in relation to the Prijedor chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So any preliminaries? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wondered if I would have the Court's permission to scout around the room and find a set of earphones, because we need an extra set over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are two here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's plenty of earphones apparently. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the General Talic team okay with earphones? You're okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are fine. We don't have any preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If you require anything, please let me know. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then Your Honour, the only matter is this: We begin today the evidence relating to the municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As Your Honours were aware, the witness who was supposed to come was taken into hospital other the break, and so we have had to reorganise. The first witness will be called by Ms. Richterova. But Your Honour, just one matter in relation to the documents. Madam Fauveau, very kindly, as is her wont, sent a letter last week indicating which particular documents in the binders were contested for the, if I can put it that way, the usual reasons. Your Honour, we've not had any document on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin setting out which documents are contested. I'd be grateful if -- either if Mr. Ackerman simply goes along with what Ms. Fauveau says. That's fine. But if there are any other specific documents that are contested, I'd be grateful if we could be given a list. And I'd prefer to have a list of the documents that are contested and not those that are not contested for the authenticity; the reason being that obviously those are the ones that we will try and deal with perhaps more than others with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I join Madam Fauveau's list and simply maintain the objection that I have made from the beginning regarding the admission of documents without proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's been settled. I think we can proceed with calling the witness. This witness does not enjoy any protective measures, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, there are no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to this witness, it's my assumption that there are no exhibits to be offered with regard to this witness, since we've received no list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I was asked to distribute a list of -- we disclosed it or we handed over it on Friday, and it was in the envelope together with other disclosures. So I apologise -- or if Mr. Ackerman hasn't opened the envelope yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, just for maybe looking at the page -- at the sheet of paper could mean anything. We were given this document with four documents, one of which arrived before the others, the documents being P986, P987, P797, and P1071.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I arrived here this morning, there was a stack of paper -- there were two huge boxes. I suppose the entire stack would be this high. And unfortunately in the 15 minutes that I had, I didn't find the one piece of paper that Ms. Richterova says I should have found. They have my e-mail address. They have my fax number. There's no reason they couldn't have given me this in a way to make it certain that I would -- and I think it's -- it's just not fair to throw something in my locker on the theory that I might find and it might not when they have the better way to get information to me and make sure that I have it. And I don't know what these exhibits are. I don't know if they're important. I don't know if I would have something that I would want to do if I'd had a chance to review them. And it's just not -- it's just not a proper way to proceed as far as I'm concerned. Obviously it was given to Your Honours in advance and you've had a chance to have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate this witness to last, to be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Today. Only today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I opened these two boxes that we received, and I'm almost sure that the list is not inside. Of course I cannot assert that because as Mr. Ackerman has said, it is a large quantity of documents and it is quite possible that this piece of paper is inside. I realised that these documents were there on Saturday evening, and I did not see this list among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This list was in a separate envelope, because we -- we knew that there were two big boxes and a separate envelope with disclosure of documents -- two documents which were disclosed, plus new order of witnesses, plus this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is this envelope, this document was not inside that envelope because I studied the contents of that envelope very closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically -- I mean, if I -- if I can try to not mediate but simplify things. One of these documents, which is 1071, is in the Serbo-Croat language and it is, from what I can understand, is either levee des corps, or postmortem examination results, and it's a thick document all relating to a number of bodies that were obviously found somewhere. That's one. The other one is an on-site investigation record. And this is the discovery of a mass grave in an underground cave. And this is 10 -- this is -- part of the same document, 1071.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would -- I actually predicted -- I knew something like this would go wrong. Would it be simpler if there aren't very many documents -- if Your Honours were to rise for 15 minutes while the Defence have a look at those documents and just tell us whether there's any real objection to us starting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would that be okay with you Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be all right, Your Honours. I'm not even sure that we'll be able to locate those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can if necessary provide immediate copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a short break of 15 minutes and take it up from there afterwards. --- Break taken at 2.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, are you happy now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have received copies of the exhibits. I've had a chance to look at them. They're largely irrelevant to the Brdjanin case, near as I can tell. The other issue that has come up, though, Your Honour, is this: It is, I think, since the beginning of this case, it has been the rule that the Prosecutor is to notify us on Thursday of the week before who the witnesses will be for the next week. And I received both a fax and an e-mail in Texas last week telling me the witnesses for this week would be 7.69 and 7.133. I was just informed a few moments ago that they also will have 7.65 and 7.105. I just learned that during this short break. And really if there's going to be such a rule, then it should be enforced; otherwise, it's a rule without any basis whatsoever. So for the record, I object to the calling of any witnesses beyond those that I receive notice of by Thursday of last week, that being 7.69 and 7.133. I think that if we're going to have such a rule, Your Honours should enforce it or just say there's no rule and they can just bring whoever they want whenever they want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may -- there are two things. The main purpose was to inform the Defence as soon as possible that the witness they thought was going to come was in fact not because he was ill. These two witnesses would replace that witness, who would have taken some time. Your Honours, it may well be that we have to spell out in chapter and verse that we're going to follow the order of witnesses. But with the greatest of respect to Mr. Ackerman, it cannot have occurred to Mr. Ackerman that we can spend five working days on two witnesses dealing with one crime base massacre. Now, if it did, I'm sorry. Your Honour, if it's necessary to say in terms every time these are the witnesses who will be called time permitting, then we'll do it. The fact is the next two witnesses -- one -- the first one will be a little bit longer because he's going to set the scene for Kljuc. The second one effectively deals with the same incident from a slightly different perspective. The third is the man who was going to testify before the break until we realised that he couldn't possibly finish before the break so -- and we said he was going to be called afterwards. And then after that we move on to the fourth witness, who is a political figure and is going to give the political events. Now, Your Honour, I'm sorry that Mr. Ackerman didn't appreciate that there was going to be more than those two witnesses. Your Honours heard the objection. Unless Your Honour rules that we can't, we propose to call these witnesses, both of whom are arriving tonight. Otherwise, if not, they'll have to go back to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think -- the first thing: History says that one must not assume that they're going to follow their list of witnesses and call them in that order. They haven't done that yet. And if one relies on that list, one does so as their own peril, because it changes constantly. And if you look at what the -- the rule at the beginning of this case was, that you notify us by Thursday of who your witnesses will be the next week. They notified us of those two witnesses, 7.69 and 7.133. And I just want -- I want it to be noted that I object to any other witnesses being called that weren't notified in accordance with that rule. I'm sure that when we start the Defence case the Prosecutor will want the same kind of -- kind of rule and want to be notified well in advance of who the Defence witnesses are going to be. It just puts us in a very difficult position to find out on the Monday morning who the witnesses will be for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision in regard to this matter is very simple and straight forward one. Number one is that the agreement that was reached in the beginning of this trial and the very early stages of this trial ought to be observed. And please henceforth -- and this would apply when it's your turn then as well -- do make sure, ensure that the Defence is notified in time, in good time. For this time what we are going to do is, things being what they are, we will go ahead with hearing these two witnesses, but we reserve the position should it become apparent to us that we should stop because of one reason or another, then we will stop. In other words, the witnesses will come, but we reserve the position. And we will decide accordingly as we go along. All right, Mr. Ackerman? So Witness 7.69, usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence in this case. But before you do so, the gentleman who is standing next to you will hand you the text of a solemn declaration to tell us the truth in the course of your testimony. And I kindly invite you to make that solemn declaration now by reading that text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. Mr. Cajic, I'll try to explain to you where you are and what will happen. You are in one of the courtrooms of this Tribunal, and you are giving evidence in a case that has been instituted against two persons, one of whom is Radoslav Brdjanin. The other one is General Momir Talic. You are a witness that has been brought forward by the Prosecution. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Agius. And I am flanked by two other Judges. On my right is Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and on my left is Judge Taya from Japan. The three persons you're seeing in front of you are the Registry. And what you should be interested about is for the time being, the three persons sitting in the front row to your right, those are the members of the Prosecution. And you will be first questioned -- be questioned by Madam Richterova from the team of the Prosecution. In the front row on your left, you see five persons. The first three represent -- the three who are nearer to you represent -- nearest to you represent the Defence team for General -- for Radoslav Brdjanin, and the last two represent the Defence team for General Talic. The system we adopt here is that you are asked a set of questions, one question after the other, by the Prosecution first. And you are supposed to or expected to answer those questions to the best of your ability, telling us always the truth. My advice to you here is not to go beyond what will be asked of you, not to get lost in details that are not asked of you. Just answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. When the Prosecution finishes with its series of questions, then the Defence team -- both Defence teams have a right to put questions to you. We call that a cross-examination. And it will be done one Defence team after another. After that, there may be a re-examination on the part of the Prosecution. Not necessarily so. And there may be some questions from the Bench, from us three Judges here. But that stands to be seen, and it depends very much on what your testimony will cover. Having said that, I now call upon Madam Richterova to start the examination-in-chief of her witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning -- good afternoon. Would you be so kind and state your --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: My name is Husein Cajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on 19 July 1961 in Biljani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are of Bosniak ethnic origin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are of Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you stated, you were born in Biljani. In which part of Biljani were you born and lived?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In Biljani, in the hamlet of Brkici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness the map called Biljani overview and enter it as an Exhibit 1070 and if we can place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: It's here, but the picture isn't very clear. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can -- you can have a look directly on the map which is on the ELMO. You don't need to have a look on the map which is on the screen. Maybe it will be easier for you.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that Biljani is comprised of several hamlets?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us on this map the hamlet in which you lived.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: It's the hamlet of Brkici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you say about the ethnic composition of Biljani as such and the hamlets which were part of Biljani?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Well, for the whole area of Biljani, I think about 75 to 80 per cent of the population was Muslim and about 20 to 25 per cent of the population were of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you state which hamlets were purely Muslims and which were purely Serbs, or which area were purely Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: The Brkici hamlet, Dzaferagici, and Botonici, and Jabukovac, these are of Muslim ethnicity. And then Polje, only one Serb lived there. In the centre of Biljani, which isn't indicated here, there were only three Serbs living there. And the village of Domazeti there were five or six Serbs who live there and the remainder of the population was of Muslim ethnicity. In Gologlavo, there were only Serbs. In Lancari, there were only Serbs too. That's Lancari and here you can't see Samardzije, Lakici, Sikmani, and these were purely Serbian villages. These villages haven't been indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any mosques or other religious buildings in the area of Biljani?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In the area of Biljani, there was one religious building. There was one mosque. And there were two auxiliary builds which served for the same purpose. The mosque was in the hamlet of Dzaferagici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these other two religious buildings?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: One religious building was in Jabukovac and the other in Poponici [phoen]. These were prominent buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember in which conditions were these religious buildings by the end -- by the middle of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In the middle of 1992, the mosque was in excellent condition. It had been renovated a few years ago whereas in Mesani and Jabukovac, and Botonici they were a little dilapidated, but they were -- the condition was correct. They were just a little bit used. The buildings were just a little bit older.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they still used?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time they were still in use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We do not need the map any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you very briefly describe the situation, the condition of living in your area, Biljani, and surrounding areas before 1990s and after 1990s. Were there any differences in the life? But very briefly.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I can say precisely up until 1985 that the relationships between all the ethnic groups were fairly good. People lived very well. There were mixed marriages. People would be best men. There were common weddings, et cetera. From 1985 to 1990, that's when things started to change a bit. And in the 1990s, with the beginning of the war in Slovenia, things came to a head and tension rose. There was tension since the JNA army, which was leaving Slovenia, mostly moved over into Bosnia and Herzegovina. One unit moved into the vicinity of our municipality, to be more precise, to the place called Laniste. And that's when matters got more complicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a war in Slovenia. And what about a war in Croatia? Did it affect the life in your area as well?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: The war in Croatia started in 1991. At the time the situation changed completely. It became completely inverted. And given that the former JNA army attempted to take parts of Croatia and before parts of Slovenia and didn't succeed in doing that, they started mobilising other forces, other troops. And among those ranks, there were Muslims. And at that time, given the relationship between the Croats and the Muslims and their co-existence, the Muslims didn't respond to the mobilisation and they were put on the side, whereas the Serbs accepted this. They accepted the mobilisation and went to the battlefield in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they accepted and went to Croatia, were mobilised, do you know whether they still received salaries in their respective jobs, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I didn't work in local factories. Since before that I worked in Slovenia and then I worked privately. I had a brother and a sister-in-law and some relatives who worked in the factory. In fact, when the mobilisation was proclaimed, they remained to work there, especially the men, whereas all the local population who worked in the factory and went to the battlefield in Croatia, they received their salaries, but they also had a salary which they received from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what were the consequences of refusing to be mobilised for the non-Serb population, or even for Serb population, refused to go to the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: For the Serbian population, no, I can't give you any precise information. I know about the Muslims who didn't respond to the mobilisation. I know that their movements were restricted. In fact, they were ordered not to leave their villages without informing the military department of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was irrelevant to people who refused to go to battlefield. When you said they were restricted of movement, was there later restriction of movement for other non-Serb population? And I am talking about the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, in the first three months of 1992, in fact, there was no restriction of movement. It was possible to move around Bosnia and Herzegovina freely, but not beyond because there were some workers who had working permits in Croatia and Slovenia and they would go there by auxiliary routes. This was in Herzegovina and through Brcko, and these were the routes they would take to go to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I am referring again to your area. You said at the beginning there were no restrictions on movement, so it -- does it mean that there was restriction on movement at some later point?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Not really real restriction of movement, since when the referendum was held in March, when Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised, then the situation changed and certain police checkpoints were erected in Sanica and Kljuc. And among the reserve military forces, there were observation posts which they put up in Gologlavo, in the area of Gologlavo, and in the area of Lunjevo and some other places that I was not able to observe. But I know this from hearsay. I saw these two places personally, since they can be seen from my house. But I didn't see the other places. But there were four or five other observation posts of this kind. And we, the inhabitants of Biljani, lived in the centre and in the valley mainly, and we were observed from above. They would try to observe us and see where we were going, what we were doing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned these checkpoints, did you personally went through any of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of times in Sanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these checkpoints were established shortly after the referendum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So shortly after the referendum, there were checkpoints. Who manned these checkpoints after the referendum?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: At the time on the main roads, at the checkpoints of the main roads, people from the police station in Sanica were there and reserve forces of the police manned the checkpoints. There were Muslims among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct to state that there were mixed patrols?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any point when the composition of these patrols would change?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The composition changed when the Serbian police -- or in fact when the police station was taken over in Sanica, in Kljuc. It was taken over by the Serbian army, or in fact at the time it was the Yugoslav Army. That's when they took over the checkpoint. There was movement on the part of the army, on the part of the troops. And on that day, I think it was between the 20th and 22nd of May, a checkpoint in Sanica was taken over, at which my relative Mujo Cajic worked. He was on duty at the checkpoint on that day. And when the -- when Tomic Milan, the police commander came, together with soldiers and other policemen who took that checkpoint over, they were ordered -- they were then ordered to go to the police station in Sanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what happened at that police station in Sanica?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In the police station in Sanica, they were offered to sign a document according to which they were to join the Serbian civilian police. First of all, they spoke to the commander about this. And finally, they refused to do this. Cajic Mujo, and the other members of the reserve police force and of the regular police force refused to do this, those who were of Muslim nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn about what you just said? Did someone -- did someone tell you about this?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: From that day onwards, we were no longer able to enter Sanica, so I didn't see that personally. But Mujo Cajic is only 30 or 40 metres away from my house. His house is 30 or 40 metres away from my house. And I've already said that he was my uncle. And a neighbour of mine, a friend of mine, also worked in the police, Avdic Sead, he had only done his military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you learned it from your uncle, is it correct to state?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, from a cousin of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will go a little bit before this -- this time. And I would like to ask you about arming of people in Biljani and surrounding area. To your knowledge, did civilians receive or buy some weapons? And I'm talking about all population. I mean Serbs and non-Serbs. To your knowledge. Do you know whether the civilians were armed?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I can personally claim, given that in 1991, while the war was still raging in Croatia, I worked in a cafe in Bravsko. MIG 91 was the name. And on one occasion, some young men came, and they asked me to make some boards, 1 metre by 1 metre, since I had the material. When I had made these boards, one of them came and then later on several of them came with automatic rifles and they themselves told me, "Oh, we have now received this and in a few days we have to go to the battlefield in Croatia. Whoever wants to volunteer can get this and we're going to train now." And they even offered me to do this. I refused to do this. This was in 1991. In 1992, given that in 1992 the battlefield in Kupres was an issue and there were quite a lot of Serbs from our area, from the area of Biljani and Sanica, and they went in a regular manner to the battlefield there, and they had been issued uniforms and weapons, so they already had this. And on several occasions we could see a helicopter which landed in Gologlavo. Naturally it had JNA marks on it. And individual Serbs, not realising what they were saying, said, "We've received -- we've had our things and now we'll see about you." And then one other thing: The Muslims, we had certain hunting weapons which had been -- which were legally possessed. If one was a hunter, this was normal, and anyone else who legally owned a pistol, well, it was normal to possess such weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will stop you now for a second. When I am reading the transcript. You said that an individual Serbs not realising what they were saying and said, "We have received -- we have had our things and now we will see about you." Can you be more specific. Did they -- what they were referring to, because this sentence doesn't make too much sense.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps in previous statements I didn't mention this. Quite a lot can't be said, you know. On each occasion -- well, I personally had a colleague with whom I would see. We were friends. We would visit each other. But they didn't tell me this personally. They told this to Dervisevic Feriz, a relative of mine. He's 70 years old now. And there were -- there was information according to which they went from house to house and delivered weapons, distributed weapons to their -- to the local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- is it correct to state that you received from somebody else an information that --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Information, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that Serb civilians were receiving weapons.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't see it by yourself.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I saw this in Gologlavo -- in Bravsko, where I worked in the cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- what did you see in that cafe?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In that cafe, as I said, a young man came to see me. He was about 20 years old. And he asked me to make this target. And then ten young men came. They were wearing civilian clothes, and they had automatic rifles with them. And they personally told me, "We've been issued with this. In a few days time, we're going to the battlefield in Croatia. And now we're going to try these weapons out. Are you coming with us?" I said no. Because there were -- I had work to do. And shortly afterwards, ten or 15 minutes later they left. And throughout the day you could hear them testing the weapons, trying out the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from this occasion, did you see any other civilians carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Only after the 30th of May, for example. In June and July, that means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In Biljani. In my village, in my hamlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I will return to what you have already started talking about. I would like to know about arming of Muslims. Do you know whether also non-Serb people had weapons and how they received these weapons?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That was true. There were automatic weapons, about ten pieces, in Biljani too. And there were some handmade weapons, so-called Kugari [phoen]. Also in Biljani, I can't give you a precise figure, but I can claim with certainty that I -- since I was some sort of a technician, they came to me personally, Serbs, whom I did not know, and they offered me weapons to buy. But about ten of our people bought them, since the police had lists of people. When they would take away weapons, they would then sell weapons and say, "I sold weapons to this person or that person, the person under this number, and that is where he can be found."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you are referring to "our people," you are referring to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: The Serbs came and would sell this, and yes, Muslims would buy them. About -- tens of Muslims, dozens of Muslims. They would get them from the Croatian battlefield mostly and would sell them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you one question in relation to takeover of Sanica police station, as you already discussed, and it was: Do you know whether the uniforms or insignia on police uniforms changed after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: As I said, I personally did not know -- witness this. But from my relative Mujo Cajic, I heard about this. When he went to the police station, they had taken off the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather of Yugoslavia, and they put out the flag of the Serbian Republic with 4-S's on it and with the white-headed eagle. And members of the other police force and Mujo confirmed this. Immediately changed the insignia on their shoulders and they got new insignia. For some of them this was -- this represented four S's. And in most cases it was the symbol of the eagle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how this eagle looked like?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: White-headed eagle, something like what Germany has on its coat of arms, something like that. Afterwards when the army passed through Biljani, I had occasion to see that emblem again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw this emblem of eagle on insignia for the army who came to Biljani?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The first time was towards the end of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... talk about that later. I was only confirming whether you saw this.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. The four S's, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We also discussed this restriction of movement when you mentioned that there were these checkpoints. To your knowledge, was there any curfew imposed in your area?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In those days, there was no curfew. I don't know whether you'll understand me, but I'd like to say that we, especially men, didn't go to Sanica because we were not allowed to go there during the daytime, not to mention at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when you said you were not allowed -- so how do you know that you were not allowed to go there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: With the takeover of the police station, on that day quite a number of workers, or rather, all the employees of Muslim ethnicity, including my brother, both men and women, were turned back from the checkpoint at Sanica and told to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he -- did they get any explanation for this procedure?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: No. They were just told that they were no longer needed. Just they said, "Go home until further notice."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, if someone -- if someone wanted to leave Biljani and go somewhere else, does that person could go freely or does he or she needed permission?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to say, because we didn't want to go anywhere nor did we have anywhere to go, because you couldn't go to Sanica and especially not to Kljuc and especially us men. No one dared go anywhere. That's the simple truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask -- I will rephrase it. But you said you couldn't go to Sanica. Was it because of the checkpoints, or did you receive any instruction that you cannot leave your village?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: At the time we had still not been told that we couldn't leave our village, but whenever we passed the checkpoint, many inhabitants of Biljani were mistreated. They were cursed, sworn at. They were still not beaten in those days, but they were harassed, provoked, and one would have to go to the police station to get a document, a piece of paper to be able toll go to Kljuc. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one last question about these checkpoints: Did you go through any of these checkpoints after the Serbs took over the police station in Sanica?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: No, and I didn't dare go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who manned these checkpoints at that time, after the -- were there still these mixed patrols or only of one nationality Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. patrols?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Only one nationality patrols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because you said that you didn't go through any of these checkpoints, how did you know there were only one nationality patrols?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I told you that my brother went to work and there was a one national patrol. My sister-in-law went to Sanica on a couple of occasions to get her salary, my brother's wife, and she personally saw workers that she used to work with in the factory who asked for her ID, though he was her neighbour and they worked together, still she needed her ID card to be able to pass through that checkpoint and go only as far as Sanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's make it absolutely clear. What was the nationality of those who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: They were of Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would return again to the weapons. You said that there were some weapons in your village, that Muslim people bought some weapons and you had some weapons from previous days. Do you know whether there were some announcements during 1992 to surrender weapons?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what date it was, between the 25th and the 27th, but I know that on one day a van arrived informing people on the loudspeaker that all Muslims owning weapons should hand over their weapons at the railway station in Sanica. Not at the police station, but at the railway station in Sanica, which was no longer being used by the railways. Of course the Muslims did that in 99 per cent of the cases on that day. But two men either didn't hear the announcement that day or for some other reason - I don't know which - but I do know that they came the next day and said, "If those two men --" and they read out the number of the rifle. One was a hunting rifle, legally owned, and the other was an automatic rifle. And "if they are not returned to the railway station, all the other Muslims would be taken into custody." And these young men did so on that day, which means that all the weapons from Biljani were handed in but I don't know exactly whether it was the 25th or the 26th of May that this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you handed over the weapons, what happened? Did anybody come to your village to check whether you really handed over the weapons?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: The next day or two days later, from the direction of Kljuc an armoured vehicle arrived in olive-grey colour, two armoured vehicles, with some 50 to 70 soldiers walking alongside them. I can confirm this personally because we first heard them arriving, these two APCs, from Kljuc to Sanica. In front of them were civilians, inhabitants of the hamlet of Cehici. And when they reached the entrance to Brkici, the crossroads there, these people reached our houses and told us that every household should hang out a white sheet on the balcony or somewhere else as a sign of recognition, as a sign of surrender, and that men between 16 and 60 years of age should walk in front of these APCs, that is, they should go to the asphalt road at the crossroads towards Sanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened with the civilians who came from Cehici?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: When we approached those APCs, when we got closer, I was able to see clearly that behind those APCs and around them, some 20 to 50 metres on each side, I saw soldiers wearing olive-grey uniforms. Some of them had camouflage uniforms. And then one of their commanders -- I don't know his name, so I can't tell you -- said to the inhabitants of Cehici that they could go home. And as we were quite numerous, that half of the inhabitants of Brkici could also go home, whereas the other half of some 30 men - and I was among them - we were ordered to walk in front of the APCs towards Sanica, which we did as far as the hamlet of Jabukovac. So we were a human shield, and we were told that. Just before we reached Jabukovac, they said to two or three men: "Go to Jabukovac, gather all men between 18 and 60 and tell them to hang out the white sheets. If all of them don't come out to the bridge at Jabukovac, we will execute these men in front." There were no incidents. No one did anything at all. We reached the bridge safely. At the bridge the people of Jabukovac were in front of us, and we were allowed to return to our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were still in Brkici and soldiers arrived to the village of Brkici --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what did they do in your village, these soldiers who arrived from this direction of probably Cehici?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Those soldiers, according to what my mother said, who stayed at home, they just passed through the village, entered the houses, looked into the stables, and then continued towards Jabukovac. Nothing happened. We returned home and the whole unit went on towards Sanica, and we stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers, can you tell us who they were, what did they -- what did they wear?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: All the soldiers were armed, normally with automatic weapons. As I said, there were two APCs, one of which I think was a PAT, P-A-T, anti-aircraft gun. They had normal weapons, just like any military unit would have, with grenades and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: -- and weapons clips and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did they wear?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I just said. They had olive-grey uniforms, and a few had camouflage uniforms. Most of these were made from the canvas used for tents by the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to notice any insignias on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many of them had the insignia of four S's, some of them on their caps had these white-headed eagles. And each of them on their epaulettes had a ribbon in a certain colour, probably this was a sign of recognition, but at the time we didn't know what it meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after these soldiers left your village and you returned to your homes, did anything else happen in your village?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In Brkici itself, nothing. But I can say on the basis of stories the next day and the day after that that same evening, from the hamlet of Polje, close to Sanica, they took 15 to 20 men to Sanica, whereas the rest were all told to return home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I learnt about this from my sister, as my sister lives in Polje, the hamlet of Polje, as they took her neighbour and another 15 or 20 young men as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any soldiers come to your village at some other occasion?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I can say that those same soldiers three days later, again from the direction of Sanica, they arrived going in the direction of Kljuc, and they once again searched the whole village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did they find something?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, they didn't find anything either. Only returning from Sanica and no one was arrested from the Brkici hamlet, from Cehici, Osmanovici, and the centre of Biljani, 20 -- or rather, 50 men were taken into custody and taken towards Kljuc. That day a killing occurred when Cehici -- I've forgotten the first name now -- Hamdo. I was a witness as the soldiers came from the direction of Gologlavo, across the hill, this is the first day, this must have been around the 1st of June. When we heard them come from Sanica, these two APCs, we turned around to face them. However, behind our backs soldiers came and ordered us to rally in the middle of the village at the intersection of roads, which we did, just the men. The women remained at home. I was present. I can't tell you the name, but working in the cafe at Bravsko, I knew a Serb and I exchanged greetings with him, and I was close to the commander of that unit. Also present was radio communications officer. And when we heard some loud shots, I said to the signalsman, "Look, go and see what's happening. They're shooting from the hill up there at ours." We said, "But that is your checkpoint, your observation post. They are shooting." And then he ordered the fighting to stop. And a couple of minutes later, he was angry. He was really angry. He started shouting and cursing, and he said that all of us inhabitants of Brkici should remain in the village, whereas he hurried on with some 30 men that he had in his units towards the centre of Biljani. And it was only the next day that we learnt that Cehic Hamdo had been killed, and we also learnt next day that 50 to 60 men had been taken from Osmanovici, Cehici, and the centre of Biljani to the school -- to the elementary school in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this and other -- this visit or search or presence of army, before 10 of July, did any group of soldiers come to your village again?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Correct. Occasionally when they went to the front lines, passing through the village from Sanica they would often shoot at the houses. Also on the 20-something of June, from the direction of Sanica, soldiers arrived. As my house is in a position that I can see the road, 1 kilometre towards Sanica and 1 kilometre towards Kljuc, we noticed soldiers coming from Sanica. And after five or ten minutes, people said, "The soldiers are coming again from Gologlavo and from Lancari," that is, from that part of our village. Just then soldiers -- reservists came. That is, the local inhabitants of Lancari. There were even some civilians among them who were armed and carrying rifles and who said that all men between 18 and 60 should come out of their houses, go to the locality of Jezerina next to our village, whereas the women and children should remain in front of the houses that, no one should remain in the houses because the soldiers would be searching the houses. We did as we were told, all of us. And when this commander arrived, he introduced himself. He said who they were and where they came from. It was a company from Lusci Palanka. The soldiers went to search the village. And when he received the report that there was no one in the village, that they hadn't found any weapons there, we entered the village together with them. Before that they had some sort of a list and they called out from that list my brother Smajo Cajic, Feriz Dervisevic, and Omer Dervisevic and they took them with them from Biljani towards Jabukovac and Polje, whereas the rest of us inhabitants of the village remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to them? Did they return or were they arrested?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: All three of them were brought back that evening around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On occasions of these searches, arrests, was ever anybody killed in your village?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I said that only Hamdo Cehic had been killed the first time. And that day we learnt immediately that Dzaferagic Abid had been killed and Tehvid Omanovic. We were told this by Boro in person. Boro and Mladjo Tesic, as they brought my brother and these other two to the village. And the next day we also heard that Hasib Mujezinovic, also known as Djuza had been killed. Then in the hamlet of Polje, another four or five men had been killed. I can't remember the names now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- you said: "On that day we learned immediately that Dzaferagici had been killed." Which day are you referring --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Dzaferagici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which day are you referring, the day when your brother was arrested?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that day. And all these killings that I just listed happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the bodies?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the bodies of the killed because I didn't dare leave the house. My late father went to fetch the bodies and to bury them at the cemetery in Cehici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one last question before we turn to the 10th of July. Did you see any SDS representatives in your village on any of these occasions?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vlado Umcanin the president of the SDS came on the day of the ultimatum for the handover of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember what did he say?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: He came another day with Ajkic Redzo who was the leader of the SDA party at the time. And he issued an ultimatum about the handover of an automatic rifle and a hunting rifle, saying if that didn't happen the whole village would pay for it. But as I said, I'm not quite sure what day that was, the 25th or the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this the only occasion when any representatives, either SDA or SDS, ever visited your village?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I think it was, because I personally was present. Only Mr. Fikret Balagic and Osman -- Balagic Fikret was secretary of Kljuc municipality. He lived in Brkici. Hamdic Osman, who worked in the military department after the handover of weapons -- I can't tell you which colonel they addressed, but they tried to arrange some kind of co-existence and they went to Sanica four or five times for talks and negotiations. And they had even come to some sort of an agreement on co-existence and the protection of Muslims, saying that no one could hurt us. Unfortunately this colonel did not live long after that. He was killed somewhere on the front, so that nothing ever came of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus on the 10th of July. And now I'm a little bit lost with the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you had been consulted. Have you consulted the Prosecution as well? The plan is to go on till 4.40. We may require one, two-minutes to change the tapes. Until then, we'll go straight to 4.40. Then we'll have a 20-minute break. We'll start -- recommence at 5.00 and we'll finish at 6.30. So we'll only have a 20-minute break between now and the end. However, if -- if that creates problems for you, madam, we could --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, it doesn't create -- I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's my fault. I thought you had been consulted, actually. So it's not a problem. I tried to economise as much as possible on breaks so that you could possibly finish with this witness today, if that was your intention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I said, now I would like to focus on the day of 10 July 1992. Can you start from the morning. What happened which -- which you remember, the first thing which struck your attention.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Let's start by saying that the first thing that I noticed was that I got up early, which is my habit. Around 6.00 I was still lying in my bed. I heard four or five shots coming from different directions. I found that suspicious, and subconsciously I thought something was wrong, as if they were making some sort of an arrangement. Then I woke another three or four men who had houses along the road but were no longer sleeping in their houses. They had withdrawn from the road to be safer, and they never spent the night in their own houses. They -- for the last two months. And when we got up, we discussed what it could be and what we should do next. We were going to cut the grass in Lancari. And the previous day the young man whose grass was to be cut had gone to ask Serbs whether we could go and cut grass and said -- and they said, "Of course. There's no problem. We will even make sure that no one will interfere with your work."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just stop you here. When you said that you asked your neighbour for permission to cut the grass, why did you do it? Was it your obligation to ask your neighbours for permission?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: We couldn't leave the village and go anywhere, because the police informed us that we were not allowed to leave the locations. We weren't allowed to go to the forest, to walk around the meadows, to go to other hamlets and walk around other hamlets. So about -- at the end of the 30th of May, our movement was restricted a hundred per cent. We weren't even allowed to go from one hamlet to another. And to go -- to cross a checkpoint, we couldn't even think about doing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we can return again back to 10 of July. You said you wanted to cut the grass. You woke up at 6.00 in the morning. And please go on.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: As I said, from the upper village Jasarevici, Enis Jasarevic, came by and he said, "Listen the village is surrounded, and we have all been ordered to gather at Jezerina." All men between the age of 18 and 60, and women and children are to remain at home, they're to go outside of their houses because the village will be searched again. Normally this is what we did. And we were among the first to head towards Jezerina. And at about 30 or 40 metres away I quite by accident looked in the direction of Jezerina, the so-called meadow, and I saw some armed soldiers there. They were on guard. They'd been positioned there. They were talking, and their rifles were pointing in our direction. I looked towards Glavica and up there I saw five or six soldiers. They were standing there too. And naturally, without thinking about this, since soldiers had already passed by and they'd cleaned up the village, well, we thought okay, we'll go to Jezerina, they can do their job, and we'll carry on as usual. When the late -- the late father, he was ill. He had diabetes. And he was at the limit -- at the age limit. He was about 60 years. I said, "Are you going?" He said, "No, you go, my son. I'll remain at home." This is what we did. I can say that at that time people under 18 years of age also came out and people who were over 60 years of age. And when we got to Jezerina when we all gathered there, behind our houses we saw Marko Samardzija immediately. I knew him very well. First of all, he was my teacher at elementary school for the first four classes. And for four years he taught me history in elementary school. We saw him first of all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cajic, can I stop you for a second again. You said you saw Marko Samardzija, who was your teacher at the elementary school. At this point what -- what was Marko Samardzija -- in which capacity was Marko Samardzija in Jezerina?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Samardzija was with Tesic Mladjo there. He was standing there with him. And when we approached them, I noticed, given that only he addressed us, I noticed a sign on Marko Samardzija. At the time it was the rank of captain. And Mladjo Tesic, I saw he had insignia. He told us that Marko Samardzija was his deputy -- I apologise, that Tesic Mladjo was his deputy. I knew him too, since we lived in the same neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could I stop you again. You are talking too fast, so please slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Within the next five minutes we will need to stop for about a minute. So whenever it's convenient for you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Within the next five minutes, we will need to stop for about two minutes to have the tapes changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you. I mean, I'm just telling you five minutes ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you saw Marko Samardzija and he had the sign for captain. What did he wear?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: He had three stars on his pocket, whereas Mladjo Tesic had three broad lines on his shoulders. And I can also mention that they had all ribbons of the same colour which had been tied to their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that he had a rank of captain. So did he wear some uniform, Marko Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Marko Samardzija was also wearing an olive-grey uniform, whereas Mladjo Tesic was in camouflage uniform. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know at that time which unit did he belong?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I didn't know which unit Marko belonged to at the time, but I do know that in -- when -- before they had moved around the battlefields and on the basis of what certain people had said, I knew that he was a company commander since that on day he was the one giving orders, saying how we would line up, saying where we would go. He provided us with all the instructions that we had to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think we can stop at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I will have a two-minute break, during which time the tapes can be changed. And then we'll continue. Everyone will remain seated, please. As soon as we have the thumbs-up sign, then we can resume. I think we can resume already. Is that correct? Yes. Madam Richterova, you may proceed. We've got very efficient technicians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that Marko Samardzija gave you some orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. First of all, Marko Samardzija, when we lined up, before we saw about another 20 soldiers who were concealed. And when we lined up, they all came out and surrounded us. Marko Samardzija first of all spoke to Fiko and Osman. I didn't hear this conversation. And then he went in front of the line-up and he said that we had been lined up there and that we would be taken to the elementary school in Biljani. We were told that we had nothing to be afraid of and that whoever was not on the list of Amer Avdic and Amer Filipovic, they would be released and that whoever was on the list would be taken to the police station in Kljuc. I think that at that time, before we headed towards the school, Mladjo said that people over 60 years of age and people under the age of 18 could return home. They were the first to leave the line-up. And then in columns, two by two, we headed in the direction of the village and passed through the village in the direction of the elementary school in Biljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were lined up and they surrounded you. Can you be more specific. Who surrounded you?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Marko Samardzija personally ordered us to line up two by two, so one behind the other. And then once we had lined up, from the surrounding hedges and from behind trees, from the shadows soldiers approached. And when they approached us, I knew them all because these were inhabitants who were wearing uniforms, olive-grey uniforms, people from Lancari and Gologlavo. I personally knew these people since this is my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know which unit these people belonged? Were they just regular -- were they regular soldiers or reserve soldiers or policemen?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I think they were from the reserve forces of the JNA army, given that these same units knew on previous occasions to go to the battlefield from the direction of Sanica, they would go to Jajce, to Bihac, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you said, you were lined up and you were ordered towards the Biljani school. What happened when you approached the school? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: About 20 or 30 metres from the school -- as we approached it, the first thing I noticed was there were quite a few soldiers there. And then in front of the shop that we had in Biljani, I saw about 20 or 30 women in front of the shop and they were surrounded by soldiers. And then as we moved on, in front of the school itself I saw a white van. And in front of that white van, there were policemen. In this case, they were wearing camouflage uniforms, all of them, and they had white belts. At that moment they were putting their belts on and their pistols and truncheons and they were putting their gloves on, because I knew one of the young men personally and one of them said, "Look, they're good soldiers. All sorts of things are going to happen here." And then 5 metres on, Marko Samardzija was going there and in front of a tree, in front of the school itself, Tomic, the commander of the police in Sanica was standing there, and another person was standing there, Marceta. I didn't know him personally. I knew him by sight. And then there was another person standing there, a couple of people. I knew the director of the factory in Sanica. He was one of the persons I knew. I can't remember his first and last name, but I knew him personally because I would go to the factory very often to buy material there. And then we continued to advance and we entered the school. We went into the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the school, the building. Was it a ground floor building with floors? How many rooms were inside?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Part of the building was on the ground floor, but above a classroom -- there were only three classrooms in the building, 2 by length and 1 across and there was a common room above one of the classrooms, the last one and the common room, there was a two-roomed flat, which was used by Slavko, who up until then had been the teacher. And his wife Tanja, they taught in that school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said, if I understand correctly, on the ground floor there were two classrooms and one common room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Three classrooms and one common room. Two classrooms were extended lengthwise, and then the third one was across. I can draw a sketch for you if you like, since I went to this school for four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this was quite -- it's quite obvious how the school looks like. You were asked -- you were ordered to the ground floor classrooms.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I still haven't said. When we entered the hall, there were about ten policemen there and they were in camouflage uniform and had white belts. They had previously searched us. And everything we had in our pockets and on us, they took all this away, our watches, for example. And then as they searched each person, they would send that person to the classroom. In the first classroom -- the first classroom was already full and the inhabitants of Brkici -- we inhabitants of Brkici filled up the second classroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- you said the first classroom was already full, so you -- were you able to look inside and tell us how many people approximately could be inside?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I can't assess this figure with precision. All I know is that all the seats had been taken. So in a classroom, there'd be up to 35 seats. I couldn't see everything, but I know that there were other people standing around against the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were ordered to the second classroom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there already some people inside of the classroom?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end, how many -- approximately how many people were inside of this second classroom?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, I think there were about 60 and something people from Brkici and at least another 30 others, since later on five or six people entered. So in my opinion, between 90 and 100 people were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this classroom was full, did you see that some other people would enter the school or were approaching the school?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Only about half an hour later through the window one young man said, since I was sitting next to the window, he said, "Here are the people from Botonici." There were about 30 people from Botonici and they were brought in next to the school -- I don't know where they went. They didn't enter the classroom where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you were inside of the classroom, what happened?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: For the first half an hour, nothing happened. And then, half an hour later, Mihic first came. I know he was the commander -- the deputy commander, since Mujo told me that he was deputy commander of the police in Sanica. And he was a mechanic, an auto mechanic, and he would often come to my house since he repaired my television. Mihic was the first to enter. He said we should calm down a little. And he said that he would compile some sort of a list and make a record and he said that we had nothing to be afraid of. And after -- first of all, he started making this list. And about ten minutes later, Lazic, a young man, turned up, also from the neighbourhood, and he was a member of the reserve forces of the police. He was wearing a blue police uniform. He carried on compiling this list. And we provided our full names and the date -- our dates of birth and the names of our fathers for this list. Once they had finished making the record, they left the premises. And in front of the premises there was a policeman in camouflage uniform who stood outside all the time. He had a rifle and he was standing at the door itself. The door was open almost all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when this policeman took all your names, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: For the next ten minutes or so -- I don't know -- a soldier entered. He only read out ten names from a list. And once he had checked the names of these people, the people responded to this -- to these names that had been read out and then he left the classroom. And then 10 or 15 minutes later, from the hall -- no one else entered any more, but from the hall we were told that -- that Mujezinovic Smail should come out.
