And a few minutes after Smail you could hear the name Domazet Hamdija being called out and then Habir and after Habir, Omer Dervisevic, and after Omer, Efriam and his two sons and then Avdic Smail and then it was Ale Cajic's turn. Ale Cajic was next to me. And when he got to the door, he intended to return. This all lasted for about 15 minutes. When he wanted to return to pick up his jacket, he told the policeman at the door that he had forgotten his jacket. The policeman told him, "You won't need it any more. You don't have to return to get it." And after each person had left --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cajic, I will stop you here because I would like to use a document. And I think we will have some discussions about this document. And I would like to leave it after the break, because I think this is the most suitable time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you. So we'll have 20-minute break, resuming sharp at 5.00, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, you can phrase your question, Madam Richterova, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In fact, I do not want to phrase --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think perhaps without the presence of Defence counsel ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are on the way. I saw them coming. I mean, we said 5.00. It's after 5.00. We've lost five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I do -- for now, I do not want to ask a question. I want to show the witness the document, which is 9.474. And it is the exhumation report which we disclosed on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please hand the witness document P1071. Is it that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, it is a document which I would like to tender into evidence under P1071. Your Honour, this is an exhumation report which will be dealt with in details by our expert witness on exhumations. And I do not want to go into any details with this witness. I only want him to confirm or not confirm names of people, whether he saw them, whether he knew them, and that's all what I want to do with this witness. This document is in B/C/S. And it has been sent for translation with the amount of documents which refers to exhumations, we are just not able to receive all translations in time. But by the time when our expert will testify, we will have all relevant translations in our hands. So I would like to ask you whether you agree that I will use this document which is only in original language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any objection forthcoming from the Defence? I think, considering that she's only going to refer to names and not to details, we can -- we can move ahead. Okay? Yes, you may proceed along the lines you've indicated and not beyond for the time being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we adjourned, you listed names of people who were called out from the corridor. Do you still remember the names you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and open -- open the document which you have in front of you. And on the right-hand bottom side, you will see numbers. And I -- I would like to go to number 145, on the right-hand bottom side. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, usher, for helping.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's also ERN number 00473481.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is body number 79. Can you read the name, please, under this number.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dervisevic Omer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the person who was called and who was on the list which was read by that policeman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- sorry to interrupt you, but I think you have to perfect this line of -- this series of questions. At this point in time, although I don't understand the language, I think while the witness has the document in front of him and he's being referred to a particular person with number 79 and the name of this person being identified by you as Omer Dervisevic, I think we need to proceed -- if you're going to ask him whether he's the same person, you need to proceed with the rest of the details contained in the first line, which is son of Feta and born, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise the question does not really follow. You know, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a question of apologising. It's a question of trying to streamline the questions -- or the system of questioning so that it makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Cajic, can you read the name and other whereabouts of that person under number 79, please.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I can read it out and I can also say that Omer Dervisevic is the son of Feta and Duda that he was born in 1964, that he is the father of two children, a son and a daughter who are now 11 and 8 years old respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen to me. Let's do it differently. When Madam Richterova refers you to a particular person or name indicated in this document, please just look at the first line or so where the name and the personal details are listed and answer the question whether you think that the person mentioned in this document is the same person that you referred to previously in your evidence before we had a break. Just say, "Yes, this seems to be the same person or I'm sure it's the same person, no, I have doubts," and then you explain why you have doubts. Do you understand me? Can you follow me? Yes, yes, I know but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand. Fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there may be some kind of an error in the transcript or translation or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question -- it's at line -- the question and answer beginning at 4825 going on to 49.1 through 5. We're talking about someone who was allegedly killed in 1992. And the transcript indicates Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that he has an eight--year-old daughter or son. I can't tell which, which -- you know, it's not possible, I don't think. So I think there must have been misinterpretation or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you referred to Omer Dervisevic and you said he was son of Feta and Duda, he was born in 1964. He was the father of two children, a son and a daughter, who are now -- how old are they now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the son is about 11 or 12 and the daughter is 8 or 9, just now, at this point in time. I'm not sure, but I do know them personally, as Omer Dervisevic's house is only 200 metres away from mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it. Let's not go into details. Go ahead, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Cajic, do you confirm -- do you confirm whether it -- it is the person who was called?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That is true. That was the person who was called out. He was the third or fourth in order. I'm not quite sure, but that is Omer Dervisevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the following page. On the top you will see the words "Usrok Smrti." Would you be so kind and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to object at this time, Your Honour, because we -- we were of understanding that only the names and the whereabouts of that person indicated who this person was were the -- were the basis of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does -- what does "Usrok Smrti" mean in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "Usrok Smrti" means the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But forget about that. Because that you're going to establish by means of an expert witness, you say. So we don't -- it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How could the witness know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if I may say one thing: In my opinion, it would be much more appropriate if we go through the -- through the witness's statement where the witness has listed the names of the persons and give us all the details that he knows about these persons and not to consult this document, because it is obvious that there is some misunderstandings. And this might be understood as indication that the certain corpse does belong to that person. For example, the corpse 81 is without a head. How can it be decided that it is this person after all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But there I don't agree with you. I don't agree with you. It could be done, the way you are suggesting. It's true. But it could also be done the way it is being done now. And it's -- the Prosecution is seeking to prove is nexus between the names that appear on this document on which then someone else will testify and the names that the witness mentioned; in other words, whether the witness recognises in the name on this -- on the face of this document the same person that he's referring to before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand fully, Your Honours. But it's the -- it's the matter of asking the witness the names and the particulars about a certain person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's proceed the way we are doing. And I will not allow the question, of course, that Madam Richterova was trying to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the second -- thank you. Move to the next name, if you're finished with this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not quite sure whether the witness answered my question, because I do not have it here. So if you allow me, I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he did answer your question. He says it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I would like you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to him, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to have a look at the page 149, which is on the right-hand bottom side. And the ERN number is 00473485. If you could have a look under the number 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's barely legible here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's barely legible. I agree but we do not have a better copy?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Cajic Ale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the whole whereabouts which are next to this name?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Cajic Ale, son of Muharem, born on the 9th of April, 1955, from Donji Biljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same person you were referring to in your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same person, the last person that left, who is my cousin and who left his jacket behind in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I will ask you last name in this series. If you could go to the page number 159, which is also marked as 00473495. And if you could have a look at the number 139. Can you read the name and the whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Domazet Hamdija, son of -- I can't see the name. Born on the 15th of April, 1946, from Donji Biljani. Yes, as the year of birth coincides. I can't read out the name of the father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That is that person, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I will move further. You said after -- what happened in the room after these persons were called out? Could you here something outside?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned that after the -- each one of these persons were led out, five or ten minutes later one could hear bursts of fire and shots. At one point the policeman who was guarding the classroom smiled and said, "You see how your Green Berets are attacking us. But we'll fix it in a moment. Don't worry. No one will hurt you. We'll get rid of them soon." And after the last one left, Mihic came again and ordered that we get ready, that five by five we would be leaving in the order when the soldier tells us we can leave. And the first groups of men started leaving in fives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were inside of the room and you said that after these people left, you could hear the burst of fire. Were you able to see something from the window?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Correct. While the men were leaving in groups of five, before Mr. Mihic came, the deputy commander of the police. In the meantime two buses arrived from the direction of Kljuc and they parked in front of the school. As I was sitting next to the window, I saw half of a bus in front of the school and I saw when another gentleman arrived wearing a blue uniform who greeted Marko Samardzija. I didn't see who else was there, but I remember that the director of the sawmill was there and some other men, five or six of them. And from the classroom I could see some men were being loaded onto the bus and being beaten in front of the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Then I saw --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will stop you. If you could speak a little bit slower for the interpreters. And I would like to ask you, you said you saw Marko Samardzija outside at the time when the buses arrived. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you by any chance know approximately what time it was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I'm not able to say. I just know that it was about half past 9.00 because according to some estimates, between 7.00 and 9.00 we were in the classroom and when we started leaving, it was about 9.00, and this went on for the next half hour or 45 minutes, so it was between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I interrupted you at the moment when you said you were able to see through the window buses and some people being beaten in front of the buses. Please go on, what more you saw.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Correct. After that I saw Mile, Bakan. Mile, also known as Bakan, I knew him. He would come to our village frequently. He took five men across the road, close to a house. And shortly after that -- or rather, throughout we could hear shooting. After a while, he came back alone. In the meantime, it was already my turn to leave the classroom, which I did, and I stood right in front of the door. In the meantime, Osman Avdic, apparently saw something and said, "Men, hurry into the buses. They'll kill us all." I was just leaving the classroom at that point in time with another five men, and I reached the hallway. There was a policeman there in camouflage uniform. And from the hallway he would let one by one pass. I didn't see anything clearly except two soldiers. When I reached the actual door, when my turn came, I managed to see through the door, which was open all the time, that the policeman in front was beating Fiko Balagic and running after him. Then I saw some 10 or 15 older men leaning against a wall across the way from the school with their hands behind their heads, and I remember a policeman saying to me, "Why did they bring you here?" And I said, "I have no idea. I haven't done anything." And then he said, "You are free to go." And as I set off, in the meantime just as I was about to leave Fiko was already entering the bus and I looked forward towards the bus and I saw the whole yard in front of the school, as I was going down the steps. Just then I again saw this same group under the linden tree and 10 or 15 policemen who had made a line up to the bus, then 20 or 30 reservists, reserve soldiers standing next to them. I also saw on the fence a friend of mine -- I'm sorry. First I saw Dragan Cvijic, who used to work in the coffee bar that I made in Kljuc. Since I knew him well, I looked him in the eye and I thought he would help me, because someone has recognised me, and he looked me in the eye. At that moment he turned his head away. And as I passed by him, I felt him turn around quickly, so I too turned around. So with the toe of his shoe, he kicked me in the ribs and also with his fist. And just then I realised that I, too, would be beaten, and I hurried between the line to get onto the bus. This lasted for about 10 or 15 seconds, the length of the bus. I don't know what they beat me with nor how, but I know I reached the door of the bus, where there was another policeman and five or six other men. He was standing on the steps of the bus, and he asked me, "Do you want to sit down?" I didn't know what to say. In the meantime, the men behind me were being beaten on the back and everywhere else. After 10 or 15 seconds - I don't remember exactly how long this went on for - I was shoved into the bus and I was ordered to go to the very back, to crawl to the back of the bus, which I did. And all I was able to see in the bus was that some people were sitting. There was no sitting room, so I sat at the very back door so that in front of me was the glass window of the bus. In front of me was Refik Avdic, and behind me Fiko Balagic. I was hurting all over, and orders were coming, "Heads down. Don't look through the window," and things like that. In the meantime, while I was inside already, I heard that they were bringing the next group, beating them. If somebody fell, they would say, "Take him away. He's not fit for anything." Then he would say, "Leave this one to me. He's mine." And there were all kinds of such things. They beat them, and all the time until the bus was packed full. I had in front of me this linden tree, this tree, and all this. And I had to watch, because I was sitting on the back seat. In the meantime, the man up front said, "There's no more room in the bus." And then I heard and saw one of the soldiers ordering us to bow our heads and lie down, and I heard when one soldier walked up to this group, I saw him walk up to this group under the linden tree and ask, "What are we going to do with the others when they can't fit into the bus?" And one of them - I don't know who - said, "Kill them all. We don't need them any more." And before that, I heard Osman being taken out and a man saying, "Leave him to me. He used to work in the military department." And I don't know what he said to him. I couldn't understand. The door of the bus closed, and after that I was not able to see anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many people were inside of this bus?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Given that I went to school in these buses, I know that there are between 45 and 55 seats and not more than 25 could have fitted in the corridor. About 75.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether the other bus was full of people as well?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time. I didn't see the other bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were inside of the bus. And what happened further?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Shortly afterwards, shooting could be heard, bursts of fire. There was noise. Then the bus left. And it hadn't -- after about 10 metres it stopped, a soldier entered again. He had a white belt on, and he wanted four strong young men. And since he went up front -- we were looking at him. We wanted to know what he wanted. He then chose first of all two men and then another two, four in all, and he told the others to bow our heads and not to move, and we did this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know any names of these four men who were taken out?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could recognise the first two men. My relative was there, Avdic Amer, and I think Mujo Zukanovic was there, since he was a big man and he had a moustache. I saw him briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after these two men were taken out, what happened further? Did the bus went on, or did you stop?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I said four men. I saw the first two men. I didn't see the other two. The bus carried on, and he immediately told the person in uniform -- it went for another 100 metres or so. And the driver at that moment for some unknown reason stopped. The bus came to a halt. A soldier entered, and he asked for another five men. However, when some of them started getting up, he said, "No, I don't want those in front. I want those at the back." The driver opened the door. Since I've already said that Fiko Balagic was sitting next to me, on the seat above the door itself Avdic Besim was sitting there and Rufad Hodzic. They were the first two to leave. And then I went out. And at that point in time I only saw Fiko behind me. I saw Fiko. We headed towards -- the bus slowed down, which was 10 metres away. And since they had told me we were going to the other bus. When I was passing by the bus -- I almost had one foot in the bus already. I looked inside and saw that there were only ten men in uniform. One of them said, "No, not here. You don't have to go in here. You're going to the back." I returned back, and I was the last person in the line. Avdic Alija was in front of me. And we moved on in this way, one in front, one behind. We passed Mehmed Avdic and went down towards his stable. And when we got to the stable, these people in front stopped and cried out, "What's this, for God's sake," something like that. And since I couldn't move on because of them, the person behind me shoved his rifle in my back and said, "Advance, you balija." These people passed by. And when it was my turn, I had a look below. There were four bodies from the previous ones I already -- I recognised Amer Avdic. And the others -- I assumed the other was Muja, and Rufad, who was the first man, when he passed over them he turned right. When I passed over, I saw Besim turning left and I followed him. We had only gone four or five steps when again a voice was heard and they said, "You balijas, stop there. You're not going to go very far," and they started shooting. With the first burst of fire I only saw Besim in front of me. I saw that he had lied down in front of me, and he collapsed. At the moment I didn't know what to do. My legs failed me or something like that happened. I threw myself down next to Besim, half a metre in front, next to Besim himself. And as I had already seen that -- they all had automatic weapons. They had double clips. They were stuck together. When they changed the clips, they started shooting again. I wasn't hit by the second burst of fire either. And the third time they continued shooting, on each occasion I was wondering what would happen, but nothing hand on that occasion either. Things calmed down a bit. In the meantime, I heard them calling from the bus and saying, "Hurry up, you people down there. We're going to head towards Kljuc now." I can also remember that another one of us was still groaning, and he cried out, "The person there to the right is still alive," and he fired a burst of fire for the fourth time. And I remember that the bullets passed over me, since there was earth falling on me. They waited for minute, and then I heard them moving away from the bodies or in fact moving away from that stable. Shortly afterwards you could hear the buses. They turned the engine on and they headed in the direction of Kljuc. In the meantime, a house was on fire in front and down below there was a house too and there was smoke which started bothering -- irritating my eyes. From all the directions, from everywhere, you could hear bursts of fires, groans, singing, all sorts of songs, and shortly afterwards, only ten minutes later, I didn't know where to go or what to do. I was quite simply paralysed. All my life unfolded in front of me in a minute. I asked myself what to do, where to go. And on the basis of previous occasions -- I know what happened in Velabici [phoen]. I know that they first of all killed the people and they were collected by -- I knew they would come and solve this too, deal with this too. In the meantime, they came singing -- I won't say at the moment whether they were soldiers or who they were. I know that they came. And since there was a cafe there, say started shooting around it, they started singing, and they started destroying the furniture. And then you could hear them moving around the house. They passed down below the house and some people called out. They said, "Have a look down here. There are others down there." And someone would say, "No, I don't want to. I've had enough today and then you heard someone say, "I'm going to set this house on fire." And another person would say, "Don't. Perhaps someone might need it." And then someone would say, "Who will need it. They don't need it anymore." And then someone replied, "We'll need it perhaps. Perhaps we would live in that house in the future. It's a pity to destroy such houses. And then all sorts of things were discussed about how many people had been killed. No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cajic, if you want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Cajic, if you need a break, I'll give you a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's fine. No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cajic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time you need us to stop, let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time you need us to stop to give you a break, let us know. If you need anything, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cajic, you mentioned that when you were taken out of the bus and you started running and they were shooting on you that Besim fell down next to you. What was his last name?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: His name was Avdic Besim. He was born either in 1967 or 1968. I'm not sure. He was also the father of two children, and his house is only 20 metres away from mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were also referring to some Fiko, which is most probably a nickname. Do you know what was the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Balagic [Realtime transcript read in error "Alagic"] Fikret, son of Arif. He was 54 or 55 years old. He was the secretary of the municipality in Kljuc. He lived in Brkici in the hamlet. Only -- his house was only 100 metres away from mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see other bodies when you stood up?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that point, once the soldiers had left, half an hour or an hour had passed by. I'm not sure. I stayed there, lying. I turned my head around a bit to see what there was behind me, and I saw -- I saw the eight bodies, all of the eight bodies. My first thought was that I had to flee. And I knew that I had to flee because they would come. I started crawling. And after half a metre or a metre I turned to look behind me and I saw that there was grass behind me. I returned a bit -- returned back and then I jumped up and went to the first tree, which was about four steps away, and I hid there. There was a small sort of wood there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will stop you here for a second. And I would like to show you the page 150 in the exhumation report, which is 00473486. A second ago -- can you have a look at the number 102. And I only want to confirm whether it was -- whether you -- we got the name you said a second ago correctly. Can you read this name and whether it is the same person you are referring to as the person who was there with you or whether it is a different name.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Balagic Fikret, son of Arif, born on the 17th of April, 1940 in Donji Biljani. So at the time he was 52 years old. So this coincides. I'm not sure for a year or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's only because in the transcript was Fikret Alagic, and I didn't know whether we got the name correctly. So it -- the correct name is Balagic Fikret.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Balagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after you stood up and crawled away, what happened? What did you see? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I turned around again just to have a look, to make sure that there was no one in the vicinity of the house. And I then saw the bodies there again. There was no one around the house, and I moved about 10 metres away from that site. I was always aware of the fact that they might come and look for me and that they would follow my trail. I only rested there for a short while and then I carried on crawling. I went to a place about 20 or 30 metres away, and I entered this area and I then heard shooting. I wasn't sure and I didn't feel secure in that place either and I continued crawling towards the river, which is about 100 metres from that place and from the site where the houses are located. I went into the cornfield which -- where I felt a little freer. And I had to carry on a bit to place myself in this cornfield and I spent the whole night there. You could hear shooting throughout the day, bursts of firing in Biljani. And I saw from that place, since the Gologlavo, certain young men went to the hamlet of Gologlavo, and I saw them passing by going to their houses and I heard them shooting all the time. I stayed there until night fell, until about 11.00 or half past 11.00, I'm not sure. And just before dusk I heard from the direction of Kljuc how some heavy vehicles were arriving. At the time I couldn't recognise them, but I know that these were lorries and excavators. And I heard someone calling out, "Come here. Come to this house so that we can collect these things here, these people here." And then afterwards you would hear another voice saying,"Come here. Come here too." And this continues until 11.00 at night. I'm not sure how -- for how long exactly, but I know that it continued late into the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after this? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: That evening I went to my house. I found my father and my family there. They asked me what had happened. At that time I wasn't able to tell them much. All I know is I said that quite a few people had been killed. I asked about my brother. I asked whether he returned. They said, "No one has been returned -- no one returned, apart from Mujo Cajic Dzaferagic Semso, Zukanovic Ismet, Omanovic Semsa, and Ismet's relative -- I don't know -- Ismet's nephew, I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Brkici?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In the morning, since I wanted to establish contact with Muja and Semso Dzaferagic, they told me that they would come to search the villages, that some soldiers would come to search the villages and they told me that I should flee from the village. This is what I did. I took clothes from my sister and I went to the nearby wood. And on that evening, late that evening, because Mujo and Semso was fleeing because someone had come to the village. You could hear the sound of an engine and shooting. They fled from the village. And since I was above the village, I wanted to have the village in front of me so that I could observe what was happening, what was being done. I went to see them. And we met there. And for the next seven days or up until ten days we spent this time without food in a cave. And -- but we were no longer able to carry on like that, so we then had to approach houses, since Mujo Cajic's house is in a prominent place, his father's house, and his house. It's in the vicinity of the wood, the first houses that were there. We approached these houses and this is where we established contact for the first time and that evening we even managed to have a shower, have a bath, and have something to eat. And shortly afterwards, three or four days later, since the commander of the police, Tomic, came to the villages. He was looking for Semso Dzaferagic and he took him to Kljuc. I stayed on with Mujo Cajic and hid in the woods, in the cornfields. And when Mujo's wife established contact - I'm not sure with whom - he too, was transferred to Kljuc, taken to Kljuc. So this continued for about a month. And I stayed in Biljani for another month. I spent this time on my own in the woods or in the vicinity of houses, where I would get food. And in September, on the 20th, I think -- or in fact, on the 10th of September, my sister got into contact with a Serb and they transferred me to Kljuc. And on behalf of other -- I took some sort of card in another person's name for a convoy for Travnik. I think I left for Travnik on the 20th of September, in a trailer which was full of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While hiding in the cornfield and the forest, were you able to observe the hamlets, villages? Did you see in which conditions were houses? Did you see what happened if anything happened, to mosques or other religious buildings in your area?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: The shooting was very intense for the first few days, on the 10th of July, and then it calmed down for a while. And quite often I heard Serbian soldiers coming to the village, looking for something. On one evening I knew and I recognised the voices of my sister and of my mother. When my mother was crying, I didn't know what was being done, but when she started crying and shouting, "Where are you take my daughter," I heard that he cursed her and my sister and said, "Go away," or something like that. And then on one evening I heard them going to Avdic Alija's house, because I was very near that house. I didn't see who it was and I can't confirm this at the moment, but I do know -- I personally know that they took a child out. I think that Buco [phoen] was the child's name. I can't remember the exact name. I've forgotten it. They took the child out. At the time the child was three or four years old. And all the time they were saying -- since he was a salesman, he had a shop there. He said -- he told his wife, "If you don't give us money, we'll kill the child." I know that she gave them something because half an hour or an hour later, after they had that quarrelled and after she had cried a lot, they left the village and the woman stayed on. I remember --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cajic, my question was slightly different. I asked you about the houses and the religious buildings. So if you would be so kind and answer this question.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's no problem. I said that for the first few days they set the houses on fire. And this was quite intense. But 15 or 20 days later, while I was sleeping in the cornfields, a loud explosion could be heard. I didn't know what was being done. I didn't know what was happening. But on the following day I heard, since I went to get food, that on that evening they had mined the mosque but they hadn't managed to destroy it. It remained intact. And from the woods and the cornfields where I hid, I spent the night in the cornfields. And in the daytime I was in the woods because it was more secure for me and I could see the entire village from there and I would know whether someone was coming to the village. I saw this on that morning. I saw the mosque and I saw that they didn't destroy it, but they had mined it. But on that day they didn't destroy it entirely. They only managed to set it on fire this was a result of the explosives. And about a day or a day afterwards -- I think it was about midnight. I heard a loud explosion. I assumed -- I guessed what this was. And I had a look towards minarets, to the tower, and it wasn't there any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were able to observe the whole village. Can you tell us what happened, if anything, to the houses.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: In the hamlet of Brkici, they only set one house on fire. But as I said, a day or two or three days after the 10th of July, I personally saw how the houses around the mosque were burning and houses around the school and in Osmanovici and in Jabukovac and in Polje. There were houses burning there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to play a video. It's an excerpt from the video which we already saw right at the beginning. It was the video taken from -- by Mazhar Inayat, and we saw it at the beginning. And this excerpt is from Kljuc. The exhibit number was or is P447. And I would like the technicians to play this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you pause it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what can we see on this picture.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Here you can see the centre of Biljani itself. This is the very centre of Biljani. And you have the place where the school was located, Mezernel [phoen], and part of the Cehici hamlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring where the school was. Can you describe it better for us. How can we recognise where this school was?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: The school is right here, where you can -- where there's an empty space in this part and for the following 25 metres. That's where the school was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it -- what is here -- what is on that place now?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: There is a monument to the mosque there, a monument to those people who were killed. And there are graves there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And graves. So maybe for the record the place with the strips is the graveyard.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct? And then there was the school. Then we can see some roads --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the road from the top to the left and to the right, where these roads are heading.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: The road from the direction of Kljuc. There is a road that comes down from -- from up and on the right it goes Dzaferagici and Osmanovici and on the left you can cross the meadow and go to Brkici, and the road in front goes towards Gornja Sanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which road were you taken by bus? Is it on this -- can we see it on this picture?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: You can see it clearly. In front of the school, when we left from there, we got to this small entrance to the main road here. And this is where they took four men off the bus. And then they continued up until --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. On the screen, on which side of the screen we can see it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, at the entrance to the school where the cultural centre is, here, in front of the centre you reach the main road from Sanica to Kljuc. And that is where the bus stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are these details important for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It was just for you to have an idea. And if we can play the video. It's very, very short. To see the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if we can see the place where the bus stopped, you can -- we can pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see it now? No?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: One could see it better earlier on. No, it's all right. We can see it now. Here's the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we pause, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what can we see now? Can we see it now?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: You can see the spot. It is on the extreme left of the screen, where we see three roads intersecting. So in the middle of the screen there's a very big house. And behind it was where the bus stopped for the second time. And behind the house is the spot where the four men were executed together with me, and before us the other four.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You can go on with the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we can stop here. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in exhumation which took place in Kljuc -- in the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I personally took part in the exhumation, as in those days I had returned to my village. I was among the first to return to my village of Brkici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many bodies were exhumed and what was the name of the location where the bodies were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was personally at the location of Laniste, where about 180 bodies were exhumed. I was also present at the exhumation that took place after that, Crvena Zemlja, or "Red Earth," where 15 bodies were exhumed, among others the body of my brother. That was the last body I took out of the pit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show you two documents. The first one is -- was pre-marked P986.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if we could place the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that you haven't seen this document before, but I will read you slowly parts of this document. And I only want you to confirm whether the actions which are described in this document are consistent with the events which occurred in Biljani. This document is dated 9 of July, 1992 and it was issued by Kljuc command, and it is an order for further operations. And it says: "I have made the following decision: Use a part of the brigade to impose a total blockade, search and mop up the territory in the sectors of Donji Biljani, Domazeti, Botonici, Jabukovac, and Brkici villages. "Readiness for operation, 0500 hours on 10 July 1992. The 2nd Battalion of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade reinforced with a reconnaissance platoon, a military police squad, and a police platoon, is to block, search, and mop up the Donji Biljani, Domazeti, Botonici, Jabukovac, Osmanovici and Brkici sectors." And the last one: "When it gets dark, the platoon is to lay ambushes and bomb the Domazeti-Osljak road. Stay there until 0500 hours on 10 July and then search and mop up Domazeti. It is to join up with other units of the 2nd infantry Battalion in the sector." And now it is unknown. Probably the school in Donji Biljani. And the very last sentence is: "The Sanica police platoon is to move along the Sanica-Jabukavac-Donji Biljani route and establish a checkpoint in the sector of the Donji Biljani school for processing suspicious persons." As you remember, were these places under the search and mop-up of the army?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I can say with regard to the village of Brkici that it was mopped up in detail and that every male between 18 and 60 was detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just noticed that we've got the English version on the ELMO so that the accused can't see the document we're talking about. I thought we were putting the other one on there these days so they could see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't following the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we discussed this before. Last time we were in closed session; it didn't matter. But there are members of the public here. They can follow what everybody is talking about. So I'm afraid the accused will have to be given by their counsel copies of the documents if they want to follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner is right, Mr. Ackerman. If we can -- when we are in closed session and we can go round that, we do. But when we are in open session, I'm afraid this is how it has to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to show the witness the second document, which was pre-marked as Exhibit P986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is the same situation. I know that you haven't seen this document, but I only want you to tell us whether it is consistent with what really happened. So this document is an official note. And it's an official note dated the 10th of July, 1992. And it says that it was compiled in the Sanica SRM, which is reserve police station. Further it says: "On the evening of 9 July 1992, I was informed by the commander of the battalion quartered in Sanica that on the 10th of July his units would undertake a mopping-up operation of the terrain, meaning the area of the villages Gornji Biljani and Donji Biljani." It further says: "On 10th of July, in the early morning hours, the military units began the action, which included clearing out these villages along with the hamlets of Jabukovac, Botonici, Brkici, Osmanovici, Mesani, and Domazeti. It was planned to put the military prisoners in the area school in Biljani." And the last sentence -- last but one: "We were in constant communication with organs of the military authorities. At the end of their action it was agreed they would send two buses from Kljuc to take the prisoners back to Kljuc, which was done." The same -- the same question: Does it reflect the reality as you remember?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in connection with this document, I would like to clarify two points. It's obvious that the police, apart from military, was involved in the operation. And you mentioned that you saw the police in front -- in front of the school. Would you be so kind and describe once again for us, what did this -- was it military police or normal police? First question.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I said already that I saw the commander of the ordinary police in Sanica, Tomic Milan; then Mihic, his deputy; and also Lazic, who used to work in Sanica. And the mentioned police, military police from Kljuc was wearing camouflage uniforms and they had white belts. So this was the military police, which was in front. And I also saw the commander of the Sanica police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they had white belts. Did you notice something else about these military policemen? Did they wear something else which would strike your attention?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I repeated that they all wore camouflage uniforms, that most of them wore red berets, that they were slightly better armed than others, that all of them had truncheons, and some of them - and this I found strange - I saw for the first time they wore black gloves with the fingers cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second question: This document says "take the prisoners back to Kljuc," and the document -- and the same document is mentioning -- is talking about military prisoners. Was there any resistance in Biljani to your knowledge, military resistance of non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN CAJIC
utterances.text: I personally can confirm that in Biljani, from the beginning of May until the 10th of July, among Muslims not a single bullet was fired, that weapons were not found on any one of them. And I can claim with responsibility that not one of them ever uttered a nasty word to the Serbs, to the soldiers, or to anyone at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Who's going to go first? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't discussed it but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could read it in your eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We thought we would not be at this point today. So whatever Your Honour wishes, I'm prepared to do, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if we could utilise the next 15 minutes. First of all, let's deal with it like this: Mr. Ackerman, do you intend to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe I have no questions of the witness, Your Honour. I -- I might learn in the next few minutes that I do, but right now I would say that I don't. I haven't had a chance to speak with my client since we've heard this later testimony. Right now I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are intending to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because your colleague is consulting with your client. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to have some time to consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. This is what I was going -- because I would rather that these consultations do not take place in the courtroom itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think -- I think we will adjourn now and resume tomorrow morning at -- tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say only one thing. Because again I must apologise, my fault, but I didn't inform the witnesses that I am using with the witness tomorrow one document, and it is the same as I used today, which is P1071, this exhumation report from Laniste 1. Nothing else. And I am also using one photograph, which is also relating to this exhumation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do you need to consult with your client now so that -- I'm asking you this question so that arrangements for transportation of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is entirely -- it is entirely -- if we can do it now, it would be much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is -- I'm asking you so that the arrangements for the transportation is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We need 20 minutes, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank you all. And we will resume tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. No, no, I think he goes out first. Usher, please escort the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you, and good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
